blocks.text: Paul’s defense joins resurrection, a clear conscience, and his later discussion with Felix about righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment. Acts presents these scenes in its own later narrative and trial-setting language; they should not be treated as verbatim transcripts of Paul or as wording interchangeable with an earlier letter such as First Corinthians. The comparison is interpretive and remains debated.

The chapter’s language of resurrection and judgment should not flatten distinct concerns such as physical death, ethical agency, grief, transformation, and accountability into one formula. In this scene, judgment remains accountable and forensic rather than a means of extracting fear, coercing others, or concealing political abuse.

Acts survives in early papyri and major Greek manuscripts with differing textual profiles. Codex Bezae and related versional witnesses preserve a notably distinctive form of Acts, often called the Western text; its individual readings require case-by-case judgment. Likewise, historical evaluation of Acts is best made claim by claim rather than by assigning the whole work blanket reliability or unreliability.

sections.title: A Note on the Text of Acts
